region: South-western Sri Lanka — shaded wet-zone streams of the Kelani to Nilwala basins
description: Lives in slow, heavily shaded rainforest streams of Sri Lanka’s wet zone, keeping close to leaf litter and overhanging plants. Long known as Puntius titteya, it was placed in its own genus Rohanella in 2023; courting males flush deep cherry red.

region: Northern India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan & Afghanistan — lakes and slow rivers of the Indus, Ganges & Brahmaputra
description: A hardy subtropical barb of lakes, ponds and slow rivers across the north of the Indian subcontinent, comfortable in water as cool as 18 °C. Breeding males turn rosy red with black-tipped fins and drive females through fine-leaved plants, where hundreds of adhesive eggs are scattered.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Northern India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan & Afghanistan — lakes and slow rivers of the Indus, Ganges & Brahmaputra)
description: A long-established line-bred strain of the rosy barb in which every fin grows long and trailing. Its biology matches the wild fish, but the flowing fins slow it down and attract nippers.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Northern India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan & Afghanistan — lakes and slow rivers of the Indus, Ganges & Brahmaputra)
description: A captive colour strain selected for intense red body colour and highly reflective scales, so that even females carry a pink-orange flush. Behaviour and care are those of the wild rosy barb.

region: South-western Sri Lanka — shaded, clear rainforest streams of the Kelani to Nilwala basins
description: Endemic to shaded, clear forest streams in Sri Lanka’s wet zone, where it forages over sand and leaf litter. In breeding dress the male’s head turns ruby red while the body darkens almost to black.

region: Central Myanmar — Chindwin & middle Ayeyarwady basins
description: Named after the city of Odessa, where it first turned up in aquaria in the 1970s, it was formally described only in 2008 from central Myanmar. Males carry a broad scarlet band along the flank and black-spotted dorsal fin; both sexes have a dark shoulder spot and tail-stem spot.

region: Northern & eastern India and Bangladesh — weedy ponds and backwaters of the Ganges & Brahmaputra
description: A tiny subtropical barb of weedy ponds and floodplain backwaters, golden with a few irregular dark blotches along the flank. It is shy, does best in a planted tank kept on the cool side, and scatters its eggs among fine-leaved plants.

region: India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan & Myanmar — ponds, slow rivers and paddy fields
description: A widespread, hardy barb of ponds and slow rivers across South Asia, silvery with a dark spot behind the gill cover and another on the tail stem (hence "two-spot barb"). Breeding males develop red in the dorsal fin, which carries rows of black spots.

region: Myanmar, Thailand, Laos & Yunnan (China) — rivers and floodplains of the Ayeyarwady, Salween & Mekong
description: A close relative of the ticto barb from rivers and floodplains of mainland Southeast Asia, silvery with a dark shoulder spot and tail-stem spot. Breeding males blush red along the flank and in the black-spotted dorsal fin.

region: South-western Sri Lanka — shaded wet-zone forest streams
description: The true Cuming’s barb: a small Sri Lankan rainforest-stream barb with two dark vertical blotches on a silvery-gold body and yellow fins. In 2008 the red-finned populations long sold under this name were split off as Pethia reval.

region: South-western Sri Lanka — shaded wet-zone forest streams
description: The red-finned "Cuming’s barb" kept by aquarists since the 1930s, recognised as a separate species only in 2008 — reval combines the Sinhala words for red and fins. It lives in shaded rainforest streams and grows to only about 3.5 cm standard length.

region: Eastern India & Bangladesh — weedy floodplain ponds and ditches
description: A dwarf barb of weedy floodplain ponds, silvery with a dark shoulder spot and a black mark on the tail stem. Mature, well-conditioned fish show the small dark spots in the dorsal fin that give the species its common name.

region: Myanmar
description: A small silvery barb from Myanmar, described in 2008 and named for the bright red upper lip of males. In courtship the scales gain fine dark edges and the male darkens to an inky blue-grey.

region: Meghalaya, north-eastern India — Khasi Hills streams
description: A small barb from hill streams in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya. Normally silvery, the male takes on a rich claret flush in breeding condition; colours show best under subdued light over a dark substrate.

region: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh & Myanmar — ponds, ditches, rice fields and slow rivers
description: One of the commonest small barbs of South Asian ponds, ditches and rice fields, silvery with a black spot at the dorsal-fin base and another on the tail stem. Breeding males flush orange-red along the flanks and fins.

region: Sri Lanka & southern India — hill and lowland streams
description: Named for its two black spots, one at the dorsal-fin base and one where body meets tail. In mature males a dark-red band runs from the eye back to the tail spot beneath a bronze-green stripe, and the iris is rimmed red.

region: West Sumatra, Indonesia — highland lakes and streams
description: A small Sumatran barb whose large, dark-edged scales form a chequerboard of dark and light patches. Displaying males show brick-red fins edged in black and spar briefly with rivals without causing harm.

region: Western Ghats, south-western India — forest streams of Kerala, Karnataka & Tamil Nadu
description: A Western Ghats stream barb whose dark vertical bars break up into irregular blotches as it matures. Adults, males especially, take on a warm melon-orange to red ground colour.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — blackwater streams and peat swamps
description: A slim, peaceful barb of acidic forest streams and peat swamps whose golden flanks are lined with several thin dark stripes following the scale rows. It is the only species in its genus.

region: Malay Peninsula, Singapore, Sumatra & Borneo — peat-swamp and blackwater forest streams
description: A shy blackwater barb of peat-swamp forest streams, golden-orange with five dark bars counting the one through the eye. It needs soft, acidic, tannin-stained water and dense cover to show its colours.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — blackwater peat-swamp forest
description: Similar to the five-banded barb but yellower, with six dark bars including the eye bar and an extra bar on the tail stem. A peat-swamp species that colours up best in soft, tannin-stained water among plants.

region: Southern Borneo (Kalimantan) — blackwater peat-swamp streams
description: A Bornean peat-swamp barb patterned with a row of dark, rhomboid blotches ringed in pale gold, like the scales of a snake. Colours are strongest in dim, tannin-stained, very soft water.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — blackwater streams and peat swamps
description: A slender, active barb of peat-swamp streams with four or five dark horizontal stripes along silvery-gold flanks. Mature males develop a reddish flush and brighter fins.

region: Southern China, Hainan, Vietnam & Laos — streams, ponds and rice paddies
description: A hardy subtropical barb of southern China and northern Indochina, olive-gold with thin, irregular dark bars and flecks. The popular gold barb is a xanthic strain of this species developed by the American breeder Thomas Schubert.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Southern China, Hainan, Vietnam & Laos — streams, ponds and rice paddies)
description: The classic gold barb — a xanthic line of the Chinese barb, once sold as "Barbus schuberti" after Thomas Schubert who developed it. Bright gold with scattered black flecks; males show red fins and a reddish belly when in condition.

region: Peninsular Malaysia & Singapore — forest streams and rivers
description: Most "clown barbs" in the trade are this Malayan species, long misidentified as the Bornean B. everetti. Juveniles are boldly blotched; adults turn orange-pink with oval dark blotches, a broken mid-flank line and bright red lower fins.

region: North-western Borneo (Sarawak) — forest streams
description: The true clown barb of Borneo, rarely exported; much of the stock sold under its name is the Malayan B. dunckeri. Orange-gold flanks carry a series of large dark blotches and the fins are washed red.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java & Borneo — clear, fast forest streams
description: A large barb of clear, flowing forest streams named for its spanner- or T-shaped markings: two dark bars on the front half and a dark band running back to the tail. Old adults become heavy-bodied and their contrast fades.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java, Borneo & neighbouring islands — hill streams to lowland rivers
description: One of the most widespread barbs of Sundaland, found from hill streams to lowland rivers. Adults are plain silver with a black spot below the dorsal fin and another at the tail base; juveniles show extra spots along the flank.

region: Sumatra & Borneo (aquarium stock is farmed in Southeast Asia)
description: The classic farmed "Sumatra barb": golden with four black bars and red-edged fins, though the true identity of aquarium stock is still debated and wild P. tetrazona is rarely traded. Kept in a large group, much of its notorious fin-nipping is directed at its own kind.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Sumatra & Borneo (aquarium stock is farmed in Southeast Asia))
description: Also sold as the moss or green tiger barb: a captive strain in which the black bars spread and merge, leaving a dark, mossy-green body with a metallic sheen. The red snout and fin edges of the wild type remain.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Sumatra & Borneo (aquarium stock is farmed in Southeast Asia))
description: A melanin-free strain of the tiger barb: the bars show only as pale white bands on a golden-cream body, with pink-red eyes and orange-red fins. Behaviour, including fin-nipping, is unchanged.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Sumatra & Borneo (aquarium stock is farmed in Southeast Asia))
description: A very pale captive strain of the tiger barb with a silvery-white body on which the bars are reduced to faint ghost marks; the fins keep a soft orange edge. Its care and temperament match the ordinary tiger barb.

region: Captive-bred (GloFish® line; wild form: Sumatra & Borneo)
description: A genetically modified tiger barb carrying a red fluorescent-protein gene derived from a marine organism, so it glows under blue "actinic" light. It keeps the black bars and the behaviour of the ordinary tiger barb.

region: Captive-bred (GloFish® line; wild form: Sumatra & Borneo)
description: A GloFish line of the tiger barb that fluoresces orange under blue light thanks to an inherited fluorescent-protein gene. It is otherwise an ordinary tiger barb, bars, nipping and all.

region: Captive-bred (GloFish® line; wild form: Sumatra & Borneo)
description: A GloFish tiger barb that fluoresces vivid green under blue light; the colour is inherited, not dyed. Its dark bands and boisterous behaviour are those of the standard tiger barb.

region: Captive-bred (GloFish® line; wild form: Sumatra & Borneo)
description: A GloFish tiger barb that carries an inherited fluorescent-protein gene giving a purple body glow under blue light. Care and temperament are identical to the ordinary tiger barb.

region: Thailand, Cambodia & the Malay Peninsula — streams and swamps
description: A smaller wild relative of the tiger barb, told apart by a black spot at the base of the dorsal fin and a mid-body bar that does not reach the belly. It turns up occasionally in the trade alongside farmed tiger barbs.

region: Borneo (Kalimantan) — forest streams
description: One of five described "tiger barb" species, with a black dorsal fin capped by a red band and red pelvic fins. Wild fish occasionally appear in the trade, which otherwise relies on farmed tiger barbs of uncertain origin.

region: Western Ghats, India — fast, rocky hill rivers of Kerala & Karnataka
description: An endangered torpedo-shaped barb of clear, well-oxygenated Western Ghats rivers, also sold as the red-line torpedo barb or roseline shark. A scarlet stripe runs from the snout to mid-body above a black lateral band; most aquarium fish are now farm-bred.

region: Chalakudy River, Kerala, India
description: Endemic to the Chalakudy River in Kerala and sometimes exported mixed with Denison barbs. It differs in having a black mark in the dorsal fin, an underslung mouth and a duller red stripe that ends at or before the dorsal-fin origin.

region: Western Ghats, southern India — rivers of Kerala, Karnataka & Tamil Nadu
description: A riverine barb of the southern Western Ghats that feeds heavily on algae along flowing riverbanks. Adults are silvery with a large black blotch above the anal fin and red-and-black tipped tail lobes; mature males grow long filaments from the dorsal-fin rays, while juveniles are barred.

region: Southern India — Kaveri basin streams of Tamil Nadu & Karnataka
description: A Western Ghats barb with three dark blotches on a silvery-green body and a violet-blue sheen on the scales. Mature males develop long filaments trailing from the dorsal fin.

region: Sri Lanka — lowland and hill streams
description: Sri Lanka’s filament barb, long treated as part of the Indian D. filamentosa. Adults are silvery with a black blotch on the tail stem and red tail lobes, and breeding males develop elongated dorsal-fin rays.

region: Thailand, Indochina, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java & Borneo — rivers and streams
description: A large, active river barb with a bright red-orange patch on the gill cover, dark-edged scales and a red tail fin bordered in black. It needs a long, well-oxygenated tank with gentle current and very clean water.

region: South-western Sri Lanka — Kelani & Nilwala river basins
description: A vulnerable Sri Lankan endemic of deep, clear, heavily shaded rainforest streams, with a bold black lateral stripe on golden-silver flanks. In the wild it feeds on filamentous algae, terrestrial insects and detritus.

region: Southern Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon & Republic of the Congo — shaded rainforest brooks
description: A tiny barb of shaded, acidic rainforest brooks in west-central Africa, beige-brown with red fins. Males from some populations, such as the Nyong basin, turn entirely blood red when breeding, while others redden only on the rear half.

region: Angola, Zambia, Namibia, Botswana & Zimbabwe — vegetated floodplains of the Zambezi & Okavango
description: A slim, active barb of weedy floodplain backwaters in south-central Africa, orange-red with numerous thin dark vertical bars. Males are slimmer and redder than females.

region: DR Congo & northern Angola — blackwater forest streams of the Congo basin
description: A tiny, delicate barb of acidic blackwater streams in the central Congo basin, with three black spots on a golden body. Males show more orange in the fins; it needs very soft, acidic water and gentle tankmates.

region: West Africa — coastal river systems from Ghana to Cameroon
description: A silvery-golden barb of West African streams; the dorsal and caudal fins are washed red-orange at the base, and the first dorsal rays carry a black spot below clear tips. It is an active, hardy shoaler.

region: West-central Africa — still, tannin-stained coastal forest streams of Nigeria & Cameroon
description: One of Africa’s smallest cyprinids, under 2 cm long, from still, tannin-stained forest streams. Its translucent body ends in a large black spot at the tail base, with red-orange at the base of the caudal lobes.

region: India, Bangladesh & Nepal — floodplain waters of the Ganges & Brahmaputra
description: A small, large-scaled floodplain barb with a bright yellow dorsal fin carrying a broad black outer band, red pelvic fins and a black spot in the anal fin. Males are a little more colourful and have a taller, extended dorsal fin.

region: Eastern India — lowland streams of the Brahmaputra drainage
description: Popular for years as the undescribed "hi-fin" or drape-fin barb before its formal description in 2009. Mature males raise a huge, sail-like yellow dorsal fin recalling the South American Crenuchus, while females keep a small yellow-and-black dorsal fin.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan — slow streams and rice paddies)
description: A line-bred zebra danio carrying a dominant long-fin mutation that makes every fin keep growing into long, flowing veils. The stripes and hardy nature are those of the wild fish, but it swims less tirelessly.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan — slow streams and rice paddies)
description: Once described as a separate species, "Brachydanio frankei", the leopard danio is a spotted zebrafish morph: a mutation in the connexin 41.8 gene breaks the blue stripes into spots. It breeds and behaves exactly like the zebra danio.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan — slow streams and rice paddies)
description: Combines the spotted leopard pattern with the dominant long-fin trait, giving a speckled zebrafish with flowing veil fins. Biology is that of the zebra danio.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan — slow streams and rice paddies)
description: A low-melanin strain in which the normally dark-blue stripes show as soft gold-grey bands on a pale golden body, while the eyes stay dark. Care is the same as for the wild zebra danio.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan — slow streams and rice paddies)
description: Lacking melanin entirely, this strain shows only faint silvery-gold iridophore stripes on a pale cream body, with pink-red eyes. It is as hardy and active as the wild zebra danio.

region: Captive-bred (GloFish® line; wild form: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan)
description: The first GloFish, sold in the United States from 2003: a zebrafish carrying a red fluorescent-protein gene, originally developed in Singapore as a pollution sensor. It glows under blue light and is otherwise an ordinary zebra danio.

region: Captive-bred (GloFish® line; wild form: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan)
description: A zebrafish line carrying an inherited green fluorescent-protein gene, so the fish glows vivid green under blue light. Stripes, hardiness and behaviour match the wild zebra danio.

region: Captive-bred (GloFish® line; wild form: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan)
description: An orange-fluorescing GloFish line of the zebrafish; the colour is a heritable transgene, not a dye. Care is identical to the ordinary zebra danio.

region: Captive-bred (GloFish® line; wild form: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan)
description: A GloFish zebrafish line that carries an inherited fluorescent-protein gene giving a blue body colour under blue light. It is as active and hardy as the wild zebra danio.

region: Captive-bred (GloFish® line; wild form: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan)
description: A purple-fluorescing GloFish line of the zebrafish. The colour is inherited from generation to generation; behaviour and care match the ordinary zebra danio.

region: Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Malay Peninsula & Sumatra — clear hill streams
description: A slim, fast danio of clear, flowing hill streams whose flanks shimmer mother-of-pearl blue-violet, with an orange-red stripe running from mid-body to the tail. Pairs scatter eggs over gravel and plants at dawn.

region: Northern Myanmar — upper Ayeyarwady basin around Myitkyina
description: A zebrafish relative from northern Myanmar known in both striped and spotted forms, the blue markings set on a golden body. Males develop strongly orange-red fins.

region: Northern Thailand, Laos & Myanmar — upland streams of the Mekong & Salween
description: A pearl-danio relative from upland streams of the Mekong and Salween basins; mature males flush rosy pink-violet over silver, while females stay silvery. A fast, active shoaler that needs swimming room and current.

region: Northern Myanmar — upper Ayeyarwady basin, Kachin State
description: A small, vividly coloured danio from northern Myanmar with dark vertical bars on the front half, bluish stripes behind and a glowing orange-red line along the flank. Its red-orange fins are tipped with white.

region: Far northern Myanmar — streams of the upper Mali Hka near Putao, Kachin State
description: Described in 2012 from a handful of streams near Putao, it resembles the glowlight danio but is redder and lives in cooler water. Like its relatives it is an accomplished jumper that slips through tiny gaps.

region: Shan State, Myanmar & northern Thailand — shallow, densely vegetated spring-fed ponds
description: Discovered in 2006 in small, weedy ponds on Myanmar’s Shan Plateau and first sold as the "galaxy rasbora". Males spar with spread fins over small patches, and eggs are scattered among fine plants or moss near the bottom.

region: Lake Inle, Shan State, Myanmar — weedy lake margins
description: Endemic to Lake Inle, where it lives among dense weed at the margins. Its blue-green body is crossed by about a dozen narrow vertical bars and ends in a dark spot at the tail base; males display to each other with spread orange fins.

region: Northern Myanmar — upper Ayeyarwady tributaries near Myitkyina
description: A small danio described in 2009: golden, with rows of dark blue spots that mature fish ring in gold, and spotted fins. Young or stressed fish look silvery with a tan back.

region: Western Myanmar — hill streams of the Rakhine Yoma, Thandwe district
description: From hill streams of the Rakhine Yoma: its blue flanks carry two rows of gold spots, with a dark spot at the tail base and an orange-edged black spot behind the gill cover. Males have orange borders to the anal and pelvic fins, females white.

region: Myanmar — pools and slow streams of the Ayeyarwady basin
description: A small zebrafish relative with dark blue stripes along the upper flank and rows of dark spots below them. It is quieter and more retiring than the zebra danio and prefers well-planted, gently flowing water.

region: Northern India, Nepal, Bhutan & Bangladesh — clear Himalayan foothill streams
description: A large danio of clear Himalayan foothill streams, named for its very long barbels. Its flanks carry a chain-like pattern of dark rings along the stripes and a dark spot behind the gill cover.

region: Southern Thailand — hill streams on the Ko Yao islands, Phang Nga Bay
description: A small steel-blue danio from island hill streams in Phang Nga Bay, with two thin golden lines along its flanks. Like the zebra danio it scatters eggs over gravel and is an active, upper-water shoaler.

region: Western Myanmar — Rakhine Yoma hill streams
description: Described in 2009 and named for its snakeskin-like pattern: six or seven brown vertical bars on the front half and two rows of small spots behind. In sunlight the plain-looking flanks flash many colours.

region: Meghalaya, north-eastern India — hill streams
description: A chain danio from hill streams of Meghalaya, with a dark spot behind the gill cover and three distinct horizontal blue stripes that sometimes run together. It grows larger than the zebra danio and needs a long tank.

region: Myanmar — hill streams
description: A zebrafish relative described in 2009 and named after the extinct quagga. It has four distinct dark stripes slanting slightly downward along the side and, unlike the zebra danio, no stripes on the tail lobes.

region: Nepal, India, Bangladesh & Myanmar — clear hill streams and rivers
description: A large, fast danio of clear hill streams with steel-blue flanks crossed by yellow stripes that break into short bars near the head. It swims constantly in open water and readily jumps.

region: Western Ghats, south-western India & Sri Lanka — fast, clear streams
description: The Malabar danio of the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka resembles the giant danio but is deeper-bodied, with blue stripes separated by golden lines. It is a strong swimmer of fast, clear streams.

region: Northern Thailand — cool hill streams of the Mae Taeng (Ping basin)
description: From cool hill streams around the Mae Taeng in northern Thailand. Its golden-orange front half is crossed by dark vertical bars that give way to a dark blue stripe toward the tail.

region: Pakistan, northern India, Nepal & Bangladesh — slow rivers of the Indus, Ganges & Brahmaputra
description: A deep-bodied, silvery danio of slow South Asian rivers, with blue-grey bars on the front half and three blue stripes separated by yellow lines that converge on the tail. It tolerates cooler water than most danios.

region: Thailand & northern Peninsular Malaysia — hill streams
description: A large danio of Thai hill streams whose violet-purple flanks carry four or five slender golden stripes, with a paler violet head and belly. It is fast and boisterous and needs a long, covered tank.

region: Southern Sri Lanka — Nilwala River basin
description: A critically endangered endemic of clear, shaded streams in the Nilwala basin of southern Sri Lanka. It is readily told by eight or nine irregular dark bars between the pectoral fin and the tail stem.

region: Lake Inle, Shan State, Myanmar
description: Endemic to Lake Inle, where it shoals among submerged vegetation in clear, hard water; sometimes placed in Devario. Adults show bright purple and blue stripes, and females are larger, fuller and less colourful than males.

region: Western Ghats, south-western India — slow lowland streams
description: A small surface-dwelling chela of the Western Ghats with a straight back, keeled belly and long pectoral fins, also sold as the orange hatchet danio. Its golden-orange flanks carry a row of dark blue spots that join into a stripe in some males.

region: Eastern India & Bangladesh — ponds, ditches and slow floodplain streams
description: A deep-keeled surface fish of quiet floodplain waters, also called the Indian hatchetfish. Its translucent silvery body has a violet lustre on the tail stem and a gold-edged black blotch at the base of the tail.

region: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Myanmar — quiet floodplain waters
description: A slender, keeled surface fish of quiet South Asian floodplain waters. In front lighting its silvery scales flash rainbow colours over a deep blue underlayer, with a greenish band along the rear half.

region: Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam & Malay Peninsula — ditches, swamps and rice fields
description: A slender surface cyprinid of ditches, swamps and rice fields with a dark, reflective midlateral stripe and very long maxillary barbels. Its enlarged, wing-like pectoral fins and leaping escapes earn the name "flying barb".

region: Southern China (Guangdong) & northern Vietnam — cool mountain streams
description: Discovered in 1932 on White Cloud Mountain near Guangzhou, it was long thought extinct in the wild until small populations were rediscovered. A hardy cool-water fish with a gold-edged dark stripe and red-and-white fins that breeds readily in planted aquaria.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Southern China (Guangdong) & northern Vietnam — cool mountain streams)
description: A xanthic captive strain of the white cloud with a pale golden body and a much-reduced dark stripe, while the red-and-white fins remain. Care is the same as for the wild form.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Southern China (Guangdong) & northern Vietnam — cool mountain streams)
description: A long-finned captive strain of the white cloud, sold as the "meteor minnow", whose dorsal, anal and tail fins grow long and flowing. Biology matches the wild fish; keep it away from nippers.

region: Central Vietnam — cool coastal hill streams
description: Described in 2001, it differs from the white cloud in its paler, grey-speckled lower body and in black and whitish lateral stripes of nearly equal width centred on the flank. Some older males grow elongated dorsal and anal fins.

region: South-eastern Thailand & Cambodia — coastal peat swamps and slow forest streams
description: A slimmer relative of the harlequin rasbora with a narrower black "lambchop" mark on a copper-orange body. Pairs spawn upside-down, pressing their eggs onto the underside of broad leaves.

region: Sumatra & Borneo — blackwater peat swamps
description: The smallest Trigonostigma, from blackwater peat swamps of Sumatra and Borneo; a glowing orange line runs above its slim black wedge. Like its relatives it lays eggs on the underside of leaves.

region: Western Thailand — lowland swamps of the Mae Klong basin
description: A critically endangered Thai rasbora known from very few localities. Its dark mark is reduced to a narrow horizontal stripe along the rear half of a pinkish-gold body.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — blackwater streams and peat swamps
description: A slender blackwater rasbora whose dark lateral stripe is topped by a glowing copper-red line; its lateral line has only a few pored scales, hence "pauciperforatum". Formerly Rasbora pauciperforata.

region: Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — slow rivers and flooded forest
description: A translucent, fast-shoaling rasbora of slow rivers and seasonally flooded forest, named for its tail: each lobe carries a black band and a white tip that flick like scissor blades as it swims.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — blackwater streams
description: A blackwater rasbora with a continuous dark stripe running from the snout through the eye to the centre of the tail, bordered above by a golden sheen. It is easily confused with similar striped rasboras such as R. jacobsoni.

region: Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam & Malay Peninsula — weedy floodplain waters of the Mekong & Chao Phraya
description: Named after Bueng Boraphet, a lake in central Thailand; a black lateral stripe with a thin gold line above runs back to a red patch at the base of the tail. A hardy, peaceful shoaler of weedy floodplain waters.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — peat-swamp blackwater
description: A large, colourful peat-swamp rasbora, orange-red to pinkish with a big dark blotch at mid-flank and a smaller one behind the gill cover. It needs soft, acidic, tannin-stained water and is often shy.

region: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Myanmar — streams, ponds and ditches
description: A widespread, hardy South Asian rasbora of streams, ponds and ditches, silvery with a sharp black stripe from the eye to the tail base. It is an energetic upper-to-midwater shoaler.

region: Thailand, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — forest streams
description: A large, fast rasbora of forest streams whose deeply forked tail lobes are washed yellow to red with black tips. It needs a long tank and a tight-fitting lid.

region: Borneo (Sarawak) — blackwater streams
description: A small Bornean blackwater rasbora with a golden body, orange fins and a blue-black stripe running almost the full length of the body. The more colourful males are slimmer than the larger, fuller-bodied females.

region: Thailand, Cambodia, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — rivers and floodplains
description: A sleek rasbora with a broad, sharply defined dark-brown stripe from gill cover to tail, separated from the darker back by a pale band. The caudal fin is washed yellow.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — rivers and floodplain waters
description: A close relative of the yellowtail rasbora, sharing its broad dark-brown midlateral stripe and pale band above it, but with a bright yellow caudal fin broadly edged in black.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Bangka, Belitung & Borneo — blackwater streams
description: Adults are unmistakable: a black stripe from the mouth through the eye breaks up behind the gill cover into two rows of black "portholes" running to the tail. The back scales are dark-edged in a criss-cross net and the tail is yellow with a dark spot at its base.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — rivers and forest streams
description: Recognised by a dark rectangular blotch at mid-flank below the dorsal fin, a dark spot at the tail base and a dark line along the anal-fin base. A larger, robust rasbora of rivers and forest streams.

region: Java & the Lesser Sunda Islands — hill and lowland streams
description: A hardy rasbora of Javan and Lesser Sunda streams, yellowish with a dark lateral stripe on the rear half bordered above by a gold line. It tolerates a wider range of water than most blackwater rasboras.

region: India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Myanmar — rivers and floodplains of the Ganges & Brahmaputra
description: A South Asian rasbora of rivers and floodplains with a blue-black stripe from eye to tail base, delicately edged above and below with metallic gold. Its dorsal and caudal fins often show red-orange.

region: Thailand, Indochina, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java & Borneo — rivers and flooded fields
description: A widespread, silvery Sundaland rasbora of rivers that moves into flooded fields in the wet season and feeds largely on algae and small invertebrates. Its scales are finely edged in brown and a silvery band runs along the flank.

region: Southern China, Laos & northern Vietnam — hill streams
description: One of the northernmost rasboras, from southern China, Laos and Vietnam, recognised by a narrow dark stripe running from the gill cover into the middle caudal rays. It prefers cooler, flowing water than its tropical relatives.

region: Thailand, Laos, Cambodia & Vietnam — Mekong & Chao Phraya basins
description: A dwarf rasbora recognised as a distinct species only in 1997, with a red spot in the dorsal fin and a dark lateral stripe on the rear half. It is undemanding and peaceful and reaches only about 3 cm standard length.

region: Central Kalimantan, Borneo — peat swamps
description: Described in 2009 from peat swamps of Central Kalimantan and named after the aquarium-fish exporter Patrick Yap. It has an iridescent black midlateral stripe topped with white, a violet sheen on the flanks and reddish unpaired fins, brightest in males.

region: West Sumatra, Indonesia — highland streams
description: A Sumatran rasbora described in 1999 and named for the fiery orange body of mature males; females are plainer and fuller-bodied. Exporters tend to ship mostly the colourful males.

region: South-western Sri Lanka — shaded rainforest streams
description: A Sri Lankan endemic of shaded, clear rainforest streams, with orange-red fins and a warm flush over a pearly body in good condition; populations vary from orange to deep red. Several former colour forms have recently been described as separate Rasboroides species.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — blackwater forest streams
description: A small, translucent rasbora with emerald-green upper eyes and a white-ringed black spot high on the dorsal fin, which gives it the alternative name hi-spot rasbora. Formerly Rasbora dorsiocellata.

region: South-western Borneo (Kalimantan) — blackwater peat swamps
description: A tiny peat-swamp fish from south-western Borneo; males are deep red with a black lateral stripe and red-and-black marked fins. It needs soft, acidic water and shows full colour only over dark substrate in subdued light.

region: Western & southern Borneo — peat-swamp blackwater
description: A tiny Bornean peat-swamp rasbora, orange-red with a dark blotch below the dorsal fin, a dark stripe behind it and a spot at the tail base; "merah" is Malay for red. It lives among plants and leaf litter in acidic, tannin-stained water.

region: Malay Peninsula, Singapore & Sumatra — peat-swamp blackwater
description: The first Boraras described and one of the larger, red-orange to pink with a big black spot at mid-flank, a smaller one above the anal fin and another at the tail base. It lives among dense vegetation in acidic peat swamps.

region: Thailand, Cambodia & Vietnam — swamps, ponds and rice-field ditches
description: A tiny rasbora of Indochinese swamps and rice-field ditches, named for the black "exclamation point": a stripe ending in a spot at the tail base. An orange-red line glows above the dark stripe in good condition.

region: North-eastern Thailand & Laos — swampy waters of the Mekong basin
description: Among the smallest Boraras, from swampy Mekong-basin waters in Thailand and Laos: translucent orange-brown with a dark midlateral stripe. Males show red in the fins when displaying.

region: Southern Thailand & northern Peninsular Malaysia — vegetated swamps and ditches
description: Described in 2011; males are deep strawberry red with a single black blotch on the flank below the dorsal fin, females paler orange. It lives in heavily vegetated swamps and ditches.

region: Western Thailand & south-eastern Myanmar — clear forest streams of the Ataran & Salween basins
description: A tiny, translucent cyprinid from clear forest streams on the Thai–Myanmar border whose body glows neon green-gold in good light. It is an active open-water shoaler that needs a tight lid. Formerly Microrasbora kubotai.

region: Myanmar & western Thailand — clear forest streams
description: A tiny, translucent cyprinid with a pale golden body and a thin dark stripe along the rear half, formerly placed in Microrasbora. It shoals actively in open water among plants.

region: Bangka, Borneo & Sumatra — peat-swamp blackwater
description: One of the smallest Southeast Asian peat-swamp fishes, with an iridescent blue-green stripe and red-orange markings that vary between populations; several forms once sold under this name have since been described as separate species. It needs very soft, acidic water.

region: Sri Lanka — lowland swamps, ponds and paddy fields
description: A tiny, translucent cyprinid of Sri Lankan lowland swamps and paddy fields with an iridescent green-gold stripe along the flank, hence its other name, glowlight carplet. Males show orange tints in the fins.

region: Mekong basin — Thailand, Laos & Cambodia; swamps and floodplains
description: A miniature scissortail from Mekong-basin swamps and floodplains, only about 3 cm long. Its slender, translucent body ends in a forked tail marked with delicate black-and-white bands.

region: Peninsular Malaysia & nearby Indonesia — peat-swamp blackwater
description: The only member of its genus, a slender peat-swamp rasbora that looks plain until kept in dim, tannin-stained water over a dark substrate, where it develops much warmer colours. It reaches about 5 cm standard length.

region: Sumatra & Bintan, Indonesia — acidic peat-swamp blackwater
description: Among the smallest fishes known: females mature at under 8 mm in peat-swamp pools whose pH can fall below 4. Its translucent, larva-like body has a reduced skeleton; it is imported and bred only by specialists.

region: Lake Inle, Shan State, Myanmar — weedy lake margins
description: A small Lake Inle endemic that shoals along weedy margins; breeding males flush pink to fiery red with an orange line along the flank, while females stay soft pink. It prefers hard, alkaline water like its home lake.

region: Lake Inle, Shan State, Myanmar
description: A nearly scaleless Lake Inle endemic, also called the Asian rummynose: breeding males are steel-blue with a bright red snout and red-tipped tail lobes, while females are silvery-olive. It shoals in open water over the lake’s weedbeds.
